issues.title: [torch.compile] Clarification/regression: Dynamo cache lookup guard eval is much slower in 2.12 vs 2.7 after `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` became always True
issues.author: mihudaner
issues.body: ### 🐛 Describe the bug We are investigating a TorchDynamo cache lookup / guard evaluation performance regression when moving a large inference model from PyTorch 2.7 to a 2.12-based build. This is not currently a correctness issue. The compiled model runs, but the runtime overhead before entering compiled regions is noticeably higher. From `TORCH_LOGS="+guards"` and local profiling, the hot frame guard evaluation / cache lookup cost increased from roughly 1 ms in 2.7 to roughly 3-4 ms in 2.12 for our large decoder-style inference workload. We also noticed that `torch._dynamo.config.inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` is deprecated in newer PyTorch and effectively always True: ```python inline_inbuilt_nn_modules = Config( default=True, justknob="pytorch/compiler:inline_inbuilt_nn_modules", deprecated=True, deprecation_message="does not do anything, inline_inbuilt_nn_modules is always True", ) ``` The related commit message says: ```text inline_inbuilt_nn_modules has defaulted to True and the False path is legacy. This makes the config a no-op (always True), emits a deprecation warning when users set it to False, and removes all dead False-path code from runtime. ``` However, we could not find a detailed public issue or design note explaining the full motivation and expected behavior changes from this deprecation. We would like to confirm whether the cache lookup / guard eval regression we observe is expected, and what guard strategy changes may explain it. ### Error logs No Python exception is required to reproduce the performance issue. Representative guard log summary: ### Versions 2.7.1 and 2.12.0 #### Observed behavior For the same large inference workload and similar Dynamo configs: ```python torch._dynamo.config.guard_nn_modules = False torch._dynamo.config.inline_inbuilt_nn_modules = True ``` we observed approximately: ```text PyTorch 2.7: hot frame Guard eval latency: ~1.36 ms PyTorch 2.12: hot frame Guard eval latency: ~5.65 ms ``` The additional 2.12 `LAMBDA_GUARD`s appear In 2.7, similar object aliasing relations were logged as `OBJECT_ALIASING`, for example: ```text OBJECT_ALIASING: L['self']._modules['layers']._modules['0'].stream_prefetch is ... ``` #### Minimal reproducer direction We can provide a small reproducer that imitates the workload pattern: 1. Many repeated `nn.Module` layers. 2. Repeated module attributes used in shape computations, such as `top_k`, `spec_len`, `block_size`, `num_heads`, `head_dim`. 3. Module tensor attributes similar to `block_table`, `fa_norm_residual`, `cur_topk_list`. 4. Shared Python objects across layers to trigger alias identity guards. #### Questions 1. What was the full motivation for deprecating `torch._dynamo.config.inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` and making it effectively always True? 2. Is the intended guidance that users should no longer try `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules=False` as a performance workaround? 3. Besides `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` becoming deprecated/no-op, what other Dynamo guard or cache lookup changes between 2.7 and 2.12 could increase runtime guard eval / cache lookup overhead for large inference graphs? 4. If no config can safely recover 2.7-like lookup overhead in 2.12, what is the recommended mitigation for large repeated-module inference models? Should users refactor code to avoid reading Python/module attributes inside compiled regions, or is there a compiler-side way to reduce repeated guards? cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @amjames @jataylo @azahed98

1. We deprecated `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` so that we don't have to continue to maintain 2 tracing paths.
2. Yes - we deemed the cost of reducing recompilations to be worth the slight additional overhead. We rewrote many guards to C++, and guard eval time hasn't been a significantly reported problem for a long time `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` was defaulted to true.
3. Can you try enabling the config `use_recursive_dict_tags_for_guards`? It's not enabled by default since it can potentially cause segfaults, but it should reduce the overhead of looking up attributes.
4. `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` only affects `nn.Module`s that are defined within PyTorch - are you adding attributes to those layers? Would it be possible to move this data to outside the inbuilt `nn.Module`?

If you could write up an actual reproducer, that would also be helpful. It is odd to me that so many `LAMBDA_GUARD`s are being created - are you able to share what they're guarding on?

comments.author: mihudaner
comments.body: Yes, DecoderLayer is a user-defined nn.Module, and the ModuleList contains 82 DecoderLayer instances. I tested: ` torch._dynamo.config.use_recursive_dict_tags_for_guards = True` but it did not produce a measurable improvement. Dynamo cache lookup remained around 4 ms, approximately the same as with the default value False. A note on the analysis below: I am not deeply familiar with Dynamo's internal guard representation, so parts of my interpretation may be incomplete. I used an AI coding agent to help classify the full guard logs and then checked the counts and representative expressions against the original logs. Please correct me if I have misunderstood the meaning or runtime cost of any guard category. For the production model's hot graph, I obtained: The total leaf guard count increased by only about 12%, while LAMBDA_GUARD increased by 12.4x and guard evaluation latency increased by 4.15x. I classified the 1,755 LAMBDA_GUARDs in 2.12 into: - 676 tensor shape/layout relationships - 660 scalar module-attribute checks - 418 object identity/alias relationships - 1 ambient guard Representative expressions include: ``` layer.input_layernorm.variance_epsilon == 1e-6 layer.self_attn.scale_fa == 0.08838834764831843 layer.self_attn.fa_norm_residual.size()[0] == input_ids._base.size()[0] layer.self_attn.block_table.size()[0] == input_ids._base.size()[0] layer.mlp.gate.cur_topk_list.stride()[0] == layer.mlp.gate.cur_topk_list.size()[1] position_ids is kv_len ``` My current interpretation is that ModuleList itself may not be the direct cause of the regression. Unrolling a large number of DecoderLayers leads to duplicated guards for nested module attributes, symbolic shapes and object relationships. It seems the performance degradation is more likely related to how these guards are represented and their evaluation overhead, rather than the total quantity of guards. Since enabling use_recursive_dict_tags_for_guards=True did not reduce the measured cache lookup time, Could these root-level relational and symbolic LAMBDA_GUARDs be out of the scope of the optimization brought by recursive dict tags?

issues.title: [Inductor] fmod/remainder with Python float scalar diverge from eager for bf16/fp16 on CPU (same class as #185517)
issues.author: notandruu
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Follow-up to #185517 / #186818, which fixed this class of divergence for `add`/`sub`. Eager CPU also casts Python float scalars to the tensor dtype for `fmod` and `remainder`, but Inductor keeps them at full precision in the compute type, producing different results at rounding boundaries. For `remainder` the divergence isn't a small epsilon — the result jumps by a full modulus:

```python
import torch

def f(x):
    return torch.fmod(x, 1.7), torch.remainder(x, 1.7)

x = torch.tensor([1.703125, -1.703125], dtype=torch.bfloat16)  # 1.703125 == bf16(1.7)
eager = f(x)
comp = torch.compile(f)(x)
print(eager[0].tolist(), eager[1].tolist())   # [0.0, -0.0]            [0.0, -0.0]
print(comp[0].tolist(), comp[1].tolist())     # [0.00312..., -0.00312...] [0.00312..., 1.6953125]
```

Eager computes `fmod(x, bf16(1.7)) = fmod(1.703125, 1.703125) = 0`; Inductor computes `fmod(1.703125, 1.7) = 0.003125` in fp32. For `remainder(-1.703125, 1.7)` the sign correction then lands a whole period away: `1.6953125` vs eager's `-0.0`.

Reproduced on 2.13.0.dev20260609, CPU (macOS arm64, also expected on Linux — same codegen path).

### Fix path

#186818 added an opt-in `round_scalars_to_tensor_dtype` flag to `register_pointwise`/`promote_constants` (extending the comparison-op rounding from #175807). Enabling it for `aten.fmod` and `aten.remainder` plus a regression test should be all that's needed. `rsub` is already covered: it decomposes to `sub`, whose lowering rounds.

Note: `mul`/`div` must NOT be included — eager CPU keeps scalars at opmath precision for those kernels (mixed-precision scalar fast paths), verified empirically while working on #186818.

cc @jansel @mlazos

### Versions

torch 2.13.0.dev20260609, CPU

issues.title: `torch.compile` cannot compile a model with a basic `LSTM`, even on latest main
issues.author: tinywisdom
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Reproduction Script
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class MyModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, rnn_dims=512):
        super().__init__()
        self.rnn = nn.LSTM(input_size=rnn_dims, hidden_size=rnn_dims, batch_first=True)

    def forward(self, x):
        h0 = torch.zeros(1, x.size(0), self.rnn.hidden_size, device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype)
        c0 = torch.zeros(1, x.size(0), self.rnn.hidden_size, device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype)
        out, h1 = self.rnn(x, (h0, c0))
        return h1  # tuple (h_n, c_n)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = MyModel().eval().to("cuda")
    input_tensor = torch.rand(1, 1, 512, dtype=torch.float32).to("cuda")

    try:
        with torch.no_grad():
            eager_output = model(input_tensor)
        print("Eager output:", eager_output[0].shape, eager_output[1].shape)
    except Exception as e:
        print(e)

    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model, fullgraph=True, backend="inductor")
        with torch.no_grad():
            compiled_output = compiled_model(input_tensor)
        print("Compiled output:", compiled_output[0].shape, compiled_output[1].shape)
    except Exception as e:
        print(e)
```

### Error logs

## Output on Stable (2.7.1) and Latest `main` (2.9.0a0+gitfcc682b)

<details> <summary>Output (Stable)</summary>

```
Eager output: torch.Size([1, 1, 512]) torch.Size([1, 1, 512])
TorchDynamo purposely graph breaks on RNN, GRU, LSTMs

from user code:
   File "for_test.py", line 10, in forward
    h0 = torch.zeros(1, x.size(0), self.rnn.hidden_size, device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype)
```

</details> 

<details> <summary>Output (main branch)</summary>

```
Eager output: torch.Size([1, 1, 512]) torch.Size([1, 1, 512])
Attempted to wrap RNN, GRU, or LSTM
  Explanation: Dynamo does not support RNN, GRU, or LSTM.
  Hint: It may be possible to write Dynamo tracing rules for this code. Please report an issue to PyTorch if you encounter this graph break often and it is causing performance issues.

  Developer debug context: LSTM(512, 512, batch_first=True)

from user code:
   File "test_coverage/for_test.py", line 10, in forward
    h0 = torch.zeros(1, x.size(0), self.rnn.hidden_size, device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype)
```

</details>

## What’s Confusing?
+ This model runs just fine under eager execution.

+ It’s a very basic LSTM-based model, and doesn’t use anything exotic or fused.

+ Yet torch.compile breaks, even on the latest main (torch==2.9.0a0+gitfcc682b).

+ I understand some ops are not supported yet — but shouldn't a warning or fallback happen, instead of an outright failure? Or is there some plan to support nn.LSTM and friends via fake tensor rules in the future?

Both `torch==2.9.0a0+gitfcc682b` and `torch==2.7.1a0+gitfcc682b` have the same problem.

comments.author: XAheli
comments.body:
Investigated on latest `main` (`2.13.0a0+git795be92`, CUDA H200) with my agent. Sharing runtime-traced findings that recharacterize the problem.

### Finding 1: `allow_rnn=True` works. dynamo traces LSTM/GRU successfully

With `torch._dynamo.config.allow_rnn = True`, dynamo bypasses the `builder.py` isinstance block and **successfully traces through** LSTM and GRU forward methods. The resulting FX graph keeps `aten.lstm` as a single op:

```
1-layer LSTM (h=5, seq=3):   12 FX nodes → compiled in 0.7s   [output matches eager (atol=1e-4)]
1-layer GRU  (h=5, seq=3):   compiled in 1.0s         [output matches eager (atol=1e-3)]
```

The compiled model's outputs match eager within normal float32 precision (~1e-4), and recompilation produces **exact bitwise matches**, confirming determinism.

### Finding 2: The reported "hang" is not in dynamo it's in inductor's `compile_fx`

For larger models, the issue isn't dynamo failing to trace — it's the inductor backend taking extremely long to lower the `aten.lstm` op. The FX graph stays small even for 6-layer LSTMs:

| Config | FX nodes | `compile_fx` time | Status |
|--------|----------|-------------------|--------|
| 1L, h=5, seq=3 | 12 | 0.7s | pass |
| 1L, h=64, seq=32 | 12 | 18.8s | pass |
| 2L, h=64, seq=16 | 16 | 5.6s | pass |
| 6L, h=256, seq=64 | **32** | **79.9s** | barely |
| 1L, h=256, seq=128 | 12 | >60s | timeout |
| 6L, h=256, seq=512 | 32 | >120s | timeout |

The FX graph for a 6-layer LSTM is only **32 nodes** (25 placeholders, 6 call_functions, 1 output), yet inductor's `compile_fx` spends 80 seconds. Timeout tracebacks consistently land in inductor subsystems: `scheduler.py:_can_fuse`, `pattern_matcher.py:_match`, and `graph.py:get_dep_size_hint`.

This is a separate inductor performance issue — the `aten.lstm` op's decomposition/lowering inside inductor produces a much larger internal graph that these passes struggle with.

### Finding 3: Without `fullgraph=True`, graph break recovery is broken

Related to #141184: when `allow_rnn=False` (default) and `fullgraph` is not set, dynamo graph-breaks on the LSTM but then **fails to compile any subgraph at all** — neither pre-LSTM nor post-LSTM. Dynamo emits:

```
empty checkpoint - cannot resume from graph break
Failed to handle graph break gracefully. Skipping the function and falling back to eager.
```

Result: 0 compiled graphs, the entire model runs in eager.

## Summary

There are actually **three distinct issues** here:
1. **Dynamo blocks RNN by default** (`allow_rnn=False`) — intentional, but the `allow_rnn=True` escape hatch works
2. **Graph break recovery is broken** (0 graphs compiled) — tracked at #141184
3. **Inductor `compile_fx` scales poorly** for `aten.lstm` lowering — 32-node FX graph takes 80s, making multi-layer/large LSTMs practically unusable. This seems to be the actual blocker and may warrant a separate inductor issue.

## Environment

```
PyTorch: 2.13.0a0+git795be92
CUDA: 13.0
GPU: NVIDIA H200
OS: RHEL 9 (kernel 5.14.0-615.el9.x86_64)
```

issues.title: [inductor] SympifyError: cannot sympify ShapeAsConstantBuffer when nested_compile_region returns SymInt consumed by torch.full
issues.author: littsk
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When a function decorated with `torch.compiler.nested_compile_region` (which lowers to an `invoke_subgraph` HOP) **returns a SymInt** (e.g. `x.shape[0] * 2`) and the **outer** `torch.compile` graph passes that SymInt as a size argument to `torch.full` (or another `tensor_constructor`-backed op), Inductor fails during lowering with:

```
torch._inductor.exc.LoweringException: SympifyError: SympifyError:
    "cannot sympify object of type <class 'torch._inductor.ir.ShapeAsConstantBuffer'>"
  target: aten.full.default
  args[0]: [ShapeAsConstantBuffer(expr=2*s85), 8, 288]
  args[1]: 0.0
  kwargs: {'dtype': torch.float32, 'device': device(type='cuda', index=0), 'pin_memory': False}
```

### Why this happens

1. `InvokeSubgraph.create` (in `torch/_inductor/ir.py`) calls `ExternKernel.realize_input(x)` on every operand. When `x` is a `sympy.Expr`/`sympy.Boolean`/`int`, `realize_input` constructs `ShapeAsConstantBuffer(expr=x)` (see `torch/_inductor/ir.py:5959-5960`).
2. On the HOP output side, `create_output` passes `ShapeAsConstantBuffer` through unchanged when the inner subgraph returns a SymInt (`torch/_inductor/ir.py:8487-8488`).
3. The downstream consumer `aten.full` lowering enters `tensor_constructor.inner` (`torch/_inductor/lowering.py:3988`) which runs `size = [sympy.expand(s) for s in size]`. `sympy.expand` cannot sympify the `ShapeAsConstantBuffer` IR node and raises `SympifyError`.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
# python repro.py
import torch
from torch.compiler import nested_compile_region


@nested_compile_region
def gn(q: torch.Tensor):
    # Return both a tensor and a SymInt -- the SymInt is the trigger.
    return q.sin().cos() * 2.0, q.shape[0] * 2


@torch.compile(fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)
def fn(q: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    h, s2 = gn(q)
    # ``torch.full`` reaches ``tensor_constructor.inner``; ``s2`` is wrapped
    # as ``ShapeAsConstantBuffer(expr=2*s)`` at the HOP boundary, and
    # ``sympy.expand`` on that IR node raises ``SympifyError``.
    scratch = torch.full((s2, 8, 288), 0.0, dtype=h.dtype, device=h.device)
    return h.sum() + scratch.sum() * 0.0


q = torch.randn(128, 64, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(q, 0)
loss = fn(q)
loss.backward()
```

Notes on the reproducer:

* The HOP must return a SymInt (returning only tensors does not trigger the bug, because no `ShapeAsConstantBuffer` flows out of the HOP).
* The consumer must use `torch.full` (or `torch.zeros`/`torch.ones` etc., which all go through `tensor_constructor`). `torch.empty` does **not** trigger this -- it goes via `aten.empty_strided -> _full` and bypasses `tensor_constructor.inner`'s `sympy.expand` site (it has its own at `lowering.py:4108` but that one is on a `_full` pointwise that has already realized the size from the IR).
* The bug also reproduces inside backward graphs -- this is how it was originally hit in a real model (LLM layer wrapped with outer `torch.compile`, attention block wrapped with inner `nested_compile_region`; AOT autograd partitioner saved an outer backed SymInt as a HOP output, and `aten.full` in the backward consumed it).

### Expected vs actual

* **Expected**: lowering succeeds; the SymInt is treated as the underlying sympy expression for size computation.
* **Actual**: `SympifyError` aborts compile.

### Suggested fix

Unwrap `ShapeAsConstantBuffer` to its underlying `.expr` (a `sympy.Symbol` or `sympy.Expr`) inside `tensor_constructor.inner`, before the `sympy.expand` step. PR submitted: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/182276 (will be linked once opened).

A more general fix could be made at the HOP boundary (e.g. `ExternKernel.realize_input` not wrapping size-bound SymInts) or by making `ShapeAsConstantBuffer` sympify-able (by adding a `_sympy_` method that returns `self.expr`). Happy to refactor in either direction based on maintainer preference.

### Versions

* PyTorch: `2.9.1` (also reproduces against `main` -- structurally identical code at `torch/_inductor/lowering.py:3988`)
* CUDA: `13.1`
* GPU: NVIDIA GB200 (also reproduces on H100 in our internal runs)
* OS: Debian GNU/Linux 12 (aarch64)
* Python: 3.11.2

issues.title: [compile] Handle shallow_copy_data_ device mutation in ProxyTensor instead of save/restore workaround
issues.author: mlazos
issues.body:
## Summary

During `make_fx` tracing and `FakeTensorProp`, in-graph `shallow_copy_data_` (used for cross-device `tensor.data = ...`) mutates the `fake_device` attribute on input FakeTensors. This requires a save/restore workaround in `graph_capture.py` and `compile_fx.py` to prevent the backend compiler from seeing incorrect input devices.

## Current workaround

We save `fake_device` on all FakeTensor args before `make_fx` / `FakeTensorProp`, then restore them after. See:
- `torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/graph_capture.py` (make_fx tracing)
- `torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py` (FakeTensorProp)

## Desired behavior

Handle `shallow_copy_data_` correctly in ProxyTensor, following how `t_()` works:

- ProxyTensor snapshots placeholder `meta["val"]` via `set_meta` -> `extract_val` -> `snapshot_fake` -> `fast_detach`, creating an independent FakeTensor copy
- The live FakeTensor gets mutated by the op, but the placeholder snapshot is unaffected
- `track_tensor_tree` updates the proxy slot to point at the mutation node

The snapshot mechanism should already protect placeholder metadata (sizes, strides, storage_offset) since `fast_detach` creates a new TensorImpl via `aten.detach`. However, `fake_device` is a Python attribute on the FakeTensor wrapper, not on the TensorImpl. The `fast_detach` path does capture `fake_device` at snapshot time (`FakeTensor(fake_mode, out, x.device)`), so placeholder snapshots should be independent.

The remaining issue is that the arg FakeTensors themselves are mutated and reused after `make_fx` returns. This may require either:
1. Confirming the snapshot mechanism is sufficient and removing the placeholder restoration (keeping only arg restoration)
2. Making `shallow_copy_data_`'s FakeTensor kernel not mutate in-place during tracing

Dynamo graph inputs may need a separate fix since they don't go through ProxyTensor's snapshot path.

issues.title: Flex Attention produces NaN with `torch.compile(flex_attention, dynamic=True)` and batch-dependent mask closures
issues.author: Neronjust2017
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When wrapping `flex_attention` with `torch.compile(dynamic=True, fullgraph=True)`, we observe NaN in attention output during training with `create_block_mask(_compile=False)`

This suggests the compiled Triton kernel for `flex_attention` introduces a numerical bug ? when combined with: 
- `dynamic=True` (symbolic shapes)
- `fullgraph=True`
- Batch-dependent BlockMask (varying sparsity pattern per iteration)

## Key Code

### Mask (batch-dependent)

`mf` mask allows visual tokens to see future tokens (but not answer tokens):

```python
MOD_VISUAL = 0   # visual token
MOD_TEXT   = 1   # question text token
MOD_ANSWER = 2   # answer text token

def create_mf_mask(sample_id_map, modality_map):
    def mask_mod(b, h, q_idx, kv_idx):
        same_sample = sample_id_map[q_idx] == sample_id_map[kv_idx]
        q_is_visual = modality_map[q_idx] == MOD_VISUAL
        kv_is_visual = modality_map[kv_idx] == MOD_VISUAL
        kv_is_question = modality_map[kv_idx] == MOD_TEXT

        past_causal = q_idx >= kv_idx
        future_v2v = (q_idx < kv_idx) & q_is_visual & kv_is_visual
        future_v2q = (q_idx < kv_idx) & q_is_visual & kv_is_question

        return same_sample & (past_causal | future_v2v | future_v2q)
    return mask_mod
```

### BlockMask creation + compiled flex_attention

```python
B, L, H, D = query_states.shape

q = query_states.transpose(1, 2)  # [B, H, L, D]
k = key_states.transpose(1, 2)

    H=None,
    Q_LEN=L,    # L is varying per batch
    KV_LEN=L,
    BLOCK_SIZE=128,
    _compile=False,
)

compiled_flex_attn = torch.compile(

issues.title: Inductor: `unsqueeze` lowering loses source-tensor strides when source has non-standard layout — produces fused Triton kernel that  reads OOB
issues.author: jianweif
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

  When a `torch.library.custom_op` returns a tensor with non-standard strides, and a downstream chain of `unsqueeze → expand → contiguous → view → permute → view` ops fuses with another input plus a bias
  into a single Triton kernel, Inductor's lowering of that chain reads the source custom_op output with **stride multipliers that match a standard-contiguous layout, not the actual allocated strides**.

This will cause  
 - **Silent wrong numerics:** `max_abs ≈ 9.0` between eager and compile at production shape (vs `fp16` ULP of `~5e-4`). 100% reproducible.
 - **`cudaErrorIllegalAddress`:** rare; ~1 in 20 trials when `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` is *not* set (fragmented allocator increases the chance the racy read lands in an unmapped page)

  ### Direct evidence (from a real reproducing run)

  From the Inductor `call()` wrapper for the failing graph:

  ```python
  # Allocation honours register_fake's unusual strides:
  buf139 = empty_strided_cuda(
      (1, 2048, 120, 45, 80),
      (884736000, 120, 1, 19660800, 245760),   # T innermost, then C, W, H, B
      torch.float16,
  )
  ```

  FX annotations recorded by Inductor in the same wrapper file:

  ```
  %add_27      : "f16[1, 2048, 120, 45, 80][884736000, 120,    1,    19660800, 245760]"
  %unsqueeze_2 : "f16[1, 2048, 1, 120, 45, 80][884736000, 432000, 432000, 3600, 80, 1]"
                                                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                                                standard-contiguous; doesn't match add_27
  ```

  `unsqueeze` should be metadata-only — it should preserve all existing strides. But the post-`unsqueeze` strides are computed as `(2048*1*120*45*80, 1*120*45*80, 1*120*45*80, 45*80, 80, 1)`, ignoring `add_27`'s actual stride pattern.

  `cuda-gdb` on the captured coredump pinpoints the faulting load:

  ```
  CUDA Exception: Warp Illegal Address
  PC: 0xffe325e3b800
  Kernel: triton_poi_fused__to_copy__unsafe_view_add_clone_convolution_expand_permute_unsqueeze_view_15
  Source: <kernel>.py:28
    tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (80*(x1 // 2) + 3648*x2 + 437760*(((x0 % 2)) // 2)
                            + 437760*(x1 % 2) + 875520*x3 + (x0 // 2)), ...)
  ```

### A minimal repro script
```
import os

os.environ.setdefault("PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF", "expandable_segments:True")

import torch


# Custom op that returns a tensor with a non-standard stride layout
# (T-axis innermost, B outermost). Inductor sees this stride from
# register_fake and is supposed to honour it when lowering downstream ops.
@torch.library.custom_op(
    "reprolib::opaque_strided",
    mutates_args=(),
)
def opaque_strided(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    B, C, T, H, W = x.shape
    # Strides: (B=C*T*H*W, C=T, T=1, H=C*T*W, W=C*T) — T innermost.
    strides = (C * T * H * W, T, 1, C * T * W, C * T)
    out = torch.empty_strided((B, C, T, H, W), strides, dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device)
    out.copy_(x)  # logical values match x; physical layout differs.
    return out

@opaque_strided.register_fake
def _opaque_strided_fake(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    B, C, T, H, W = x.shape
    strides = (C * T * H * W, T, 1, C * T * W, C * T)
    return torch.empty_strided((B, C, T, H, W), strides, dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device)


def pixel_shuffle_add(x, conv_out, bias):
    """Mirror the buggy chain: pixel-shuffle x from (B, 2C, T, H, W) to
    (B, C, T, 2H, 2W) via the unsqueeze→expand→contiguous→reshape chain;
    pixel-shuffle conv_out from (B, 4C, T, H, W) to (B, C, T, 2H, 2W) via
    the simpler reshape→permute chain; sum both plus a per-channel bias.

    Inductor fuses ALL THREE reads into one Triton kernel, and that fused
    kernel reads x with stride multipliers that don't match x's actual
    (non-standard) strides.
    """
    B, C2, T, H, W = x.shape
    C = C2 // 2

    # Pixel-shuffle x: (B, 2C, T, H, W) → (B, C, T, 2H, 2W) via the
    # unsqueeze → expand → clone → view → permute → view idiom.
    x_unsq = x.unsqueeze(2)  # (B, 2C, 1, T, H, W)
    x_exp = x_unsq.expand(B, 2 * C, 2, T, H, W)  # broadcast new dim
    x_cl = x_exp.contiguous()  # materialise (1.77 GB at prod)
    x_v1 = x_cl.reshape(B, 4 * C, T, H, W)
    x_v2 = x_v1.reshape(B, C, 2, 2, T, H, W)
    x_perm = x_v2.permute(0, 1, 4, 5, 2, 6, 3).contiguous()
    x_out = x_perm.reshape(B, C, T, 2 * H, 2 * W)

    # Pixel-shuffle conv_out: (B, 4C, T, H, W) → (B, C, T, 2H, 2W).
    co_v = conv_out.reshape(B, C, 2, 2, T, H, W)
    co_perm = co_v.permute(0, 1, 4, 5, 2, 6, 3).contiguous()
    co_out = co_perm.reshape(B, C, T, 2 * H, 2 * W)

    return x_out + co_out + bias.view(1, C, 1, 1, 1)

def chain(latent: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # 1. Opaque op produces a non-standard-strided tensor.
    add_27 = torch.ops.reprolib.opaque_strided(latent)

    # 2. A second, normally-strided tensor (in the real graph this is the
    #    output of a conv3d that expanded channels 4×).
    B, C2, T, H, W = add_27.shape
    C = C2 // 2
    conv_out = torch.empty(
        (B, 4 * C, T, H, W), dtype=add_27.dtype, device=add_27.device
    )
    conv_out.normal_()

    # 3. Bias broadcast over (1, C, 1, 1, 1).
    bias = torch.zeros(C, dtype=add_27.dtype, device=add_27.device)

    return pixel_shuffle_add(add_27, conv_out, bias)

def main():
    # Production shape that triggers consistently. Smaller shapes may not.
    SHAPE = (1, 2048, 120, 45, 80)
    print(f"shape={SHAPE}", flush=True)
    x = torch.randn(*SHAPE, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda")

    print("--- eager ---", flush=True)
    eager_out = chain(x).detach()
    print(
        f"eager NaN={eager_out.isnan().sum().item()} "
        f"range=[{eager_out.float().min():.4f}, {eager_out.float().max():.4f}]"
    )

    print("--- compiled ---", flush=True)
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    compiled_chain = torch.compile(chain, mode="default")
    compiled_out = compiled_chain(x).detach()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(
        f"compiled NaN={compiled_out.isnan().sum().item()} "
        f"range=[{compiled_out.float().min():.4f}, {compiled_out.float().max():.4f}]"
    )

    diff = (eager_out.float() - compiled_out.float()).abs()
    max_abs = diff.max().item()
    mean_abs = diff.mean().item()
    print(f"diff: max_abs={max_abs:.4f} mean_abs={mean_abs:.6f}")
    # fp16 ULP at ~1.0 is ~5e-4. Anything above ~0.01 is the bug.
    assert max_abs < 0.01, (
        f"INDUCTOR STRIDE BUG: eager vs compiled diverge by {max_abs:.2f} "
        f"(expected < 0.01 for fp16 ULP)."
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

issues.title: `torch.compile` produces different classification output for model using E8M0 bit-manipulation quantization (`view(int32) → bitshift → clamp → uint8`)
issues.author: prorrice
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.compile` with `inductor` backend produces numerically different classification logits for a model that includes E8M0 (8-bit exponent-only) quantization via direct bit manipulation. The model reinterprets float32 tensors as int32 (`x.view(torch.int32)`), extracts exponent bits via bitwise shift, applies ceiling rounding based on mantissa, clamps, and converts to uint8. The classification output after quantization differs between eager and compiled modes.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import os
os.environ["TRITON_BACKENDS_IN_TREE"] = "1"

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class E8M0QuantizationBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels=16, out_channels=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=1)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)

    def e8m0_quantize(self, x):
        x = x.contiguous()
        x_bits = x.view(torch.int32)
        biased_exp = (x_bits >> 23) & 0xFF
        mantissa = x_bits & 0x7FFFFF
        needs_round_up = mantissa != 0
        e8m0_biased = biased_exp + needs_round_up.to(torch.int32)
        e8m0_biased = torch.clamp(e8m0_biased, 0, 255)
        return e8m0_biased.to(torch.uint8)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = self.bn1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        quantized = self.e8m0_quantize(x)
        x = quantized.to(torch.float32)
        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = self.bn2(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        return x, quantized


class MultiScaleE8M0Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(32)
        self.quant_block1 = E8M0QuantizationBlock(32, 64)
        self.pool1 = nn.MaxPool2d(2)
        self.quant_block2 = E8M0QuantizationBlock(64, 128)
        self.pool2 = nn.MaxPool2d(2)
        self.quant_block3 = E8M0QuantizationBlock(128, 256)
        self.global_pool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(256, num_classes)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        x, q1 = self.quant_block1(x)
        x = self.pool1(x)
        x, q2 = self.quant_block2(x)
        x = self.pool2(x)
        x, q3 = self.quant_block3(x)
        x = self.global_pool(x)
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        logits = self.fc(x)
        return logits, (q1, q2, q3)


device = "cuda"
torch.manual_seed(42)
model = MultiScaleE8M0Model().to(device).eval()
x = torch.randn(4, 3, 64, 64, device=device)

# Eager
with torch.no_grad():
    eager_logits, eager_quants = model(x)

# Compiled
torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(model, backend="inductor")
with torch.no_grad():
    comp_logits, comp_quants = compiled(x)

# Compare
diff = (eager_logits - comp_logits).abs().max().item()
print(f"Logits max diff: {diff}")
print(f"Match: {torch.allclose(eager_logits, comp_logits, atol=1e-5)}")
# Expected: max_diff > 0.1 — significant mismatch
```

### Behavior summary

| Component | Eager | `torch.compile` | Consistent? |
|-----------|-------|-----------------|-------------|
| Classification logits | Reference | Differs (max_diff observed) |  **No** |
| E8M0 uint8 encoding | Reference | May differ due to float precision |  **No** |

### Root cause hypothesis

The Inductor backend's handling of `x.view(torch.int32)` reinterpretation combined with bitwise operations (`>>`, `&`) introduces precision differences in the upstream Conv2d/BatchNorm2d pipeline (similar to GELU fusion precision). These tiny float differences propagate through the discrete quantization boundary, causing different uint8 encodings and ultimately different classification outputs.


### Error logs

No error — outputs silently differ.

import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


class E8M0QuantizationBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels=16, out_channels=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=1)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)

    def e8m0_quantize(self, x):
        x = x.contiguous()
        x_bits = x.view(torch.int32)
        biased_exp = (x_bits >> 23) & 0xFF
        mantissa = x_bits & 0x7FFFFF
        needs_round_up = mantissa != 0
        e8m0_biased = biased_exp + needs_round_up.to(torch.int32)
        e8m0_biased = torch.clamp(e8m0_biased, 0, 255)
        return e8m0_biased.to(torch.uint8)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = self.bn1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        quantized = self.e8m0_quantize(x)
        x = quantized.to(torch.float32)
        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = self.bn2(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        return x, quantized


class MultiScaleE8M0Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(32)
        self.quant_block1 = E8M0QuantizationBlock(32, 64)
        self.pool1 = nn.MaxPool2d(2)
        self.quant_block2 = E8M0QuantizationBlock(64, 128)
        self.pool2 = nn.MaxPool2d(2)
        self.quant_block3 = E8M0QuantizationBlock(128, 256)
        self.global_pool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(256, num_classes)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        x, q1 = self.quant_block1(x)
        x = self.pool1(x)
        x, q2 = self.quant_block2(x)
        x = self.pool2(x)
        x, q3 = self.quant_block3(x)
        x = self.global_pool(x)
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        logits = self.fc(x)
        return logits, (q1, q2, q3)


def test_fn() -> bool:
    """Return True if NO bug (eager == compiled). False if bug present."""
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    backend = os.environ.get("TORCH_COMPILE_BACKEND", "inductor")
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    model = MultiScaleE8M0Model().to(device).eval()
    x = torch.randn(4, 3, 64, 64, device=device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        eager_logits, _ = model(x)

    with torch.no_grad():
        comp_logits, _ = compiled(x)

    return torch.allclose(eager_logits, comp_logits, atol=1e-5)

        comp_logits, comp_quants = compiled(x)

    diff = (eager_logits - comp_logits).abs().max().item()

        q_diff = (eq.to(torch.int32) - cq.to(torch.int32)).abs().max().item()

    try:

    except Exception:

I reproduced the eager-vs-compiled mismatch on current main, but comparing both sides to a float64 reference shows Inductor tracks the reference much more closely: eager-vs-compiled logits max diff 0.044124603271484375, eager-vs-fp64 max diff 0.04412189061255134, and compiled-vs-fp64 max diff 4.882071877432281e-06. The compiled quant tensors exactly matched the fp64 reference for q1/q2/q3, while eager differed. This looks like expected amplification from discrete E8M0 bit-level quantization boundaries, with eager on the less accurate side of the boundary.

issues.title: `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` silently succeeds on `torch.matmul` (≥3D) with mismatched dtypes (float16 @ float32) where eager raises RuntimeError
issues.author: Prorrrice
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.compile(backend="inductor")` silently succeeds when executing `torch.matmul` with ≥3D inputs of mismatched dtypes (`float16` and `float32`), while **eager mode correctly raises `RuntimeError: expected scalar type Half but found Float`**.

The compiled result is a `float32` tensor numerically identical to the result of explicitly casting the `float16` input to `float32` first — confirming Inductor performs an **implicit dtype promotion** that bypasses the strict same-dtype constraint of the eager kernels.

**This is NOT a timeout or numerical precision issue** — it is a behavioral inconsistency where `torch.compile` changes the semantics of an operation that should raise an error.

### Root cause

`torch.matmul` for ≥3D inputs decomposes into `torch.bmm` internally (via `aten.matmul.default` decomposition in `torch/_prims_common/wrappers.py`). The decomposition reshapes the inputs from ≥3D to 3D, then calls `tensor1_expanded.bmm(tensor2_expanded)`. Inductor's lowering of `aten.bmm` (via `@pw_cast_for_opmath` decorator and `tuned_bmm` in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`) implicitly promotes `float16 → float32` without enforcing the same-dtype constraint that the eager CUDA/CPU kernels require.

The `aot_eager` backend correctly preserves the RuntimeError, confirming the bug is specifically in Inductor's lowering path.

**Related**: `torch.bmm` (3D) has the same root cause. `torch.mm` (2D) is NOT affected — it correctly raises RuntimeError in both eager and compiled modes.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch

# 4D matmul with mismatched dtypes
a = torch.randn(2, 4, 8, 8, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(2, 4, 8, 64, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

# Eager: raises RuntimeError
try:
    out_eager = torch.matmul(a, b)
    print(f"eager: OK dtype={out_eager.dtype}")
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f"eager: ERROR — {e}")
# Output: eager: ERROR — expected scalar type Half but found Float

# Compiled with inductor: silently succeeds
torch._dynamo.reset()

@torch.compile(backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
def compiled_matmul(x, y):
    return torch.matmul(x, y)

try:
    out_compiled = compiled_matmul(a, b)
    print(f"compile: OK dtype={out_compiled.dtype}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"compile: ERROR — {e}")
# Output: compile: OK dtype=torch.float32

# Verify the compiled output is an implicit fp16→fp32 promotion
ref = torch.matmul(a.float(), b)
print(f"max diff vs explicit promotion: {(out_compiled - ref).abs().max().item()}")
# Output: max diff vs explicit promotion: 0.0
```

### Full model-level reproducer (as found by fuzzer)

This pattern arises naturally in attention models that use mixed-precision casting for numerically stable softmax:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import math

class SingleHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, embed_dim=512, num_embeddings=10000):
        super().__init__()
        self.embed_dim = embed_dim
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings, embed_dim)
        self.query_proj = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim)
        self.key_proj = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim)
        self.value_proj = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim)
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim)

    def forward(self, x):
        x_emb = self.embedding(x)
        query = self.query_proj(x_emb)
        key = self.key_proj(x_emb)
        value = self.value_proj(x_emb)
        batch_size, seq_len, embed_dim = query.shape
        query = query.view(batch_size, seq_len, 1, embed_dim).permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        key = key.view(batch_size, seq_len, 1, embed_dim).permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        value = value.view(batch_size, seq_len, 1, embed_dim).permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        query = query / math.sqrt(query.size(-1))
        attn_scores = query @ key.transpose(-2, -1)
        attn_scores = attn_scores.float()         # upcast to float32 for stable softmax
        attn_weights = torch.softmax(attn_scores, dim=-1)
        attn_weights = attn_weights.half()         # downcast back to float16
        context = attn_weights @ value             # half @ float => error in eager, OK in compile
        context = context.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(batch_size, seq_len, embed_dim)
        return self.out_proj(context)

model = SingleHeadAttention().cuda()  # model weights are float32
x = torch.randint(0, 10000, (2, 16), dtype=torch.long, device="cuda")

# Eager: RuntimeError
try:
    model(x)
    print("eager: OK")
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f"eager: ERROR — {e}")

# Compiled: silently succeeds
torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled_model = torch.compile(model, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
try:
    out = compiled_model(x)
    print(f"compile: OK dtype={out.dtype}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"compile: ERROR — {e}")
```

### Ablation

| Setting | Behavior | Consistent with eager? |
|---------|----------|----------------------|
| `backend="inductor"` | Silently succeeds (`float32`) |  **No** |
| `backend="inductor"`, `fullgraph=False` | Silently succeeds (`float32`) |  **No** |
| `backend="aot_eager"` | `RuntimeError` |  Yes |
| Eager (no compile) | `RuntimeError` |  (baseline) |
| CPU device (no CUDA) | Same bug — eager errors, compile succeeds |  **No** |
| `torch.mm(fp16, fp32)` (2D) | Both eager and compile raise `RuntimeError` |  Yes |
| `torch.bmm(fp16, fp32)` (3D) | Same bug — eager errors, compile succeeds |  **No** (same root cause) |

### Behavior summary

| Operation | Eager | `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` | Consistent? |
|-----------|-------|--------------------------------------|-------------|
| `torch.mm(fp16, fp32)` (2D) | `RuntimeError` | `RuntimeError` |  Yes |
| `torch.bmm(fp16, fp32)` (3D) | `RuntimeError` | Succeeds (`float32`) |  **No** |
| `torch.matmul(fp16, fp32)` (4D) | `RuntimeError` | Succeeds (`float32`) |  **No** |

### Discovery context

This was discovered via WhiteFox differential fuzzing on `torch._inductor.fx_passes.fuse_attention` SDPA patterns. The fuzzer-generated attention model uses an explicit mixed-precision casting pattern (from `_sfdp_pattern_9`): upcast attention scores to `float32` for stable softmax, then downcast weights to `float16` before the final `attn_weights @ value` matmul. With model weights in `float32`, the `half @ float` matmul triggers the bug.


### Error logs


**Eager mode** (correct behavior):

```
RuntimeError: expected scalar type Half but found Float
```

**`torch.compile(backend="inductor")`** (incorrect — should raise the same error):

```
(no error — silently returns torch.float32 tensor of shape [2, 4, 8, 64])
```

import os
import torch


def test_fn() -> bool:
    """Return True if NO bug (eager and compiled agree). False if bug present.

    Bug: torch.matmul(fp16, fp32) with >=3D inputs:
      - eager raises RuntimeError "expected scalar type Half but found Float"
      - torch.compile(backend="inductor") silently succeeds (returns float32)
    Returns False when eager raises but compiled does not.
    """
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    backend = os.environ.get("TORCH_COMPILE_BACKEND", "inductor")
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

    a = torch.randn(2, 4, 8, 8, device=device, dtype=torch.float16)
    b = torch.randn(2, 4, 8, 64, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)

    eager_raised = False
    try:
        torch.matmul(a, b)
    except RuntimeError:
        eager_raised = True

    def f(x, y):
        return torch.matmul(x, y)

    compiled = torch.compile(f, backend=backend, fullgraph=True)

    compiled_raised = False
    try:
        compiled(a, b)
    except Exception:
        compiled_raised = True

    if eager_raised and not compiled_raised:
        return False
    if not eager_raised and compiled_raised:
        return False
    return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    print(f"Device: {device}")
    print(f"PyTorch: {torch.__version__}")

    a = torch.randn(2, 4, 8, 8, device=device, dtype=torch.float16)
    b = torch.randn(2, 4, 8, 64, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)

    try:
        out_eager = torch.matmul(a, b)
        print(f"eager:    OK dtype={out_eager.dtype}")
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"eager:    ERROR -- {e}")

    torch._dynamo.reset()

    def _f(x, y):
        return torch.matmul(x, y)

    compiled = torch.compile(_f, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
    try:
        out_compiled = compiled(a, b)
        print(f"compile:  OK dtype={out_compiled.dtype}, shape={tuple(out_compiled.shape)}")
        ref = torch.matmul(a.float(), b)
        max_diff = (out_compiled - ref).abs().max().item()
        print(f"max diff vs explicit a.float()@b: {max_diff}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"compile:  ERROR -- {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

    try:
        ok = test_fn()

issues.title: `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` silently succeeds on `torch.bmm` with mismatched dtypes (float16 @ float32) where eager raises RuntimeError
issues.author: Prorrrice
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.compile(backend="inductor")` silently succeeds when executing `torch.bmm` with mismatched input dtypes (`float16` and `float32`), while **eager mode correctly raises `RuntimeError: expected scalar type Half but found Float`**.

The compiled result is a `float32` tensor that is numerically identical to the result of explicitly casting the `float16` input to `float32` first (i.e., `torch.bmm(a.float(), b)`) — confirming that Inductor performs an **implicit dtype promotion** that bypasses the strict same-dtype constraint enforced by the eager CUDA/CPU kernels.

**This is NOT a timeout or numerical precision issue** — it is a behavioral inconsistency where `torch.compile` changes the semantics of an operation that should raise an error.

### Root cause

The Inductor decomposition for `aten.bmm` (in `torch/_decomp/decompositions.py`) is decorated with `@pw_cast_for_opmath`, which automatically promotes lower-precision inputs (float16, bfloat16) to float32 for computation. When the decomposition returns `NotImplemented` for the general case, the Inductor lowering (`tuned_bmm` in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`) proceeds with `mm_args` which does not enforce the same-dtype constraint that the eager backend does. As a result, Inductor implicitly promotes `float16 → float32` and computes the result without error.

The `aot_eager` backend correctly preserves the RuntimeError, confirming the bug is specifically in Inductor's lowering path.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch

a = torch.randn(2, 8, 8, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(2, 8, 64, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

# Eager: raises RuntimeError
try:
    out_eager = torch.bmm(a, b)
    print(f"eager: OK dtype={out_eager.dtype}")
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f"eager: ERROR — {e}")
# Output: eager: ERROR — expected scalar type Half but found Float

# Compiled with inductor: silently succeeds
torch._dynamo.reset()

@torch.compile(backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
def compiled_bmm(x, y):
    return torch.bmm(x, y)

try:
    out_compiled = compiled_bmm(a, b)
    print(f"compile: OK dtype={out_compiled.dtype}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"compile: ERROR — {e}")
# Output: compile: OK dtype=torch.float32

# Verify the compiled output is an implicit fp16→fp32 promotion
ref = torch.bmm(a.float(), b)
print(f"max diff vs explicit promotion: {(out_compiled - ref).abs().max().item()}")
# Output: max diff vs explicit promotion: 0.0
```

### Ablation

| Setting | Behavior | Consistent with eager? |
|---------|----------|----------------------|
| `backend="inductor"` | Silently succeeds (`float32`) | ❌ **No** |
| `backend="inductor"`, `fullgraph=False` | Silently succeeds (`float32`) | ❌ **No** |
| `backend="aot_eager"` | `RuntimeError` | ✅ Yes |
| Eager (no compile) | `RuntimeError` | ✅ (baseline) |
| CPU device (no CUDA) | Same bug — eager errors, compile succeeds | ❌ **No** |
| `torch.mm(fp16, fp32)` (2D) | Both eager and compile raise `RuntimeError` | ✅ Yes |

**Key finding**: `torch.mm` (2D) correctly preserves the error in both eager and compiled modes. Only `torch.bmm` (3D batched) silently bypasses the dtype check in Inductor.

### CPU reproduction

This bug also affects CPU — it is not CUDA-specific:

```python
import torch

a = torch.randn(2, 8, 8, dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(2, 8, 64, dtype=torch.float32)

# CPU Eager: RuntimeError
try:
    torch.bmm(a, b)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f"CPU eager: ERROR — {e}")
# Output: CPU eager: ERROR — expected scalar type Float but found Half

# CPU Compiled: silently succeeds
torch._dynamo.reset()

@torch.compile(backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
def compiled_bmm(x, y):
    return torch.bmm(x, y)

out = compiled_bmm(a, b)
print(f"CPU compile: OK dtype={out.dtype}")
# Output: CPU compile: OK dtype=torch.float32
```

### Discovery context

This was discovered via WhiteFox differential fuzzing on `torch._inductor.fx_passes.fuse_attention` SDPA patterns. The fuzzer-generated attention model upcasts attention scores to `float32` for stable softmax, downcasts weights to `float16`, then performs `attn_weights.half() @ value` — which eager rejects but `torch.compile` silently accepts.


### Error logs


**Eager mode** (correct behavior):

```
RuntimeError: expected scalar type Half but found Float
```

**`torch.compile(backend="inductor")`** (incorrect — should raise the same error):

```
(no error — silently returns torch.float32 tensor of shape [2, 8, 64])
```

import os
import torch


def test_fn() -> bool:
    """Return True if NO bug (eager and compiled behave consistently).
    Return False if bug present (compiled silently succeeds where eager errors).
    """
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    backend = os.environ.get("TORCH_COMPILE_BACKEND", "inductor")

    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    a = torch.randn(2, 8, 8, device=device, dtype=torch.float16)
    b = torch.randn(2, 8, 64, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)

    # Eager: expected to raise RuntimeError due to mismatched dtypes
    eager_raised = False
    try:
        torch.bmm(a, b)
    except RuntimeError:
        eager_raised = True

    # Compiled: should raise the same RuntimeError; bug = silently succeeds
    @torch.compile(backend=backend, fullgraph=True)
    def compiled_bmm(x, y):
        return torch.bmm(x, y)

    compiled_raised = False
    try:
        compiled_bmm(a, b)
    except RuntimeError:
        compiled_raised = True
    except Exception:
        # Any other exception (e.g. BackendCompilerFailed wrapping RuntimeError)
        # — count as "raised" for our purposes
        compiled_raised = True

    # No bug: both raise (consistent). Bug: eager raises but compiled succeeds.
    return eager_raised == compiled_raised


if __name__ == "__main__":
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    print(f"Device: {device}")
    print(f"Torch: {torch.__version__}")

    a = torch.randn(2, 8, 8, device=device, dtype=torch.float16)
    b = torch.randn(2, 8, 64, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)

    # Diagnostics: show what eager does
    try:
        out_eager = torch.bmm(a, b)
        print(f"eager: OK dtype={out_eager.dtype}")
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"eager: ERROR -- {e}")

    # Diagnostics: show what compiled does
    torch._dynamo.reset()

    @torch.compile(backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
    def compiled_bmm(x, y):
        return torch.bmm(x, y)

    try:
        out_compiled = compiled_bmm(a, b)
        print(f"compile: OK dtype={out_compiled.dtype}")
        ref = torch.bmm(a.float(), b)
        print(f"max diff vs explicit fp16->fp32 promotion: {(out_compiled - ref).abs().max().item()}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"compile: ERROR -- {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

    try:
        ok = test_fn()
    except Exception:
        import traceback
        traceback.print_exc()
        os._exit(2)
    print(f"test_fn returned: {ok} (True=no bug, False=bug)")
    os._exit(0 if ok else 1)

```

issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

torch.compile fails to compile some code with complex operations, minimal example:
```python
import torch
from scipy.signal import get_window
import numpy as np

class TorchSTFT(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, device, filter_length=800, hop_length=200, win_length=800, window='hann'):
        super().__init__()
        self.filter_length = filter_length
        self.hop_length = hop_length
        self.win_length = win_length
        self.device = device
        self.window = torch.from_numpy(get_window(window, win_length, fftbins=True).astype(np.float32)).to(device)

    def transform(self, input_data):
        forward_transform = torch.stft(
            input_data,
            self.filter_length, self.hop_length, self.win_length, window=self.window,
            return_complex=True)

        return torch.abs(forward_transform), torch.angle(forward_transform)

    def inverse(self, magnitude, phase):
        inverse_transform = torch.istft(
            magnitude * torch.exp(phase * 1j),
            self.filter_length, self.hop_length, self.win_length, window=self.window)

        return inverse_transform.unsqueeze(-2)

    def forward(self, input_data):
        self.magnitude, self.phase = self.transform(input_data)
        reconstruction = self.inverse(self.magnitude, self.phase)
        return reconstruction


model = torch.compile(TorchSTFT(device='cuda'))
x = torch.randn(16000, requires_grad=True).to('cuda')
y = model(x)
y.sum().backward()

```python
import os
import torch
from scipy.signal import get_window
import numpy as np


class TorchSTFT(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, device, filter_length=800, hop_length=200, win_length=800, window='hann'):
        super().__init__()
        self.filter_length = filter_length
        self.hop_length = hop_length
        self.win_length = win_length
        self.device = device
        self.window = torch.from_numpy(
            get_window(window, win_length, fftbins=True).astype(np.float32)
        ).to(device)

    def transform(self, input_data):
        forward_transform = torch.stft(
            input_data,
            self.filter_length, self.hop_length, self.win_length, window=self.window,
            return_complex=True)
        return torch.abs(forward_transform), torch.angle(forward_transform)

    def inverse(self, magnitude, phase):
        inverse_transform = torch.istft(
            magnitude * torch.exp(phase * 1j),
            self.filter_length, self.hop_length, self.win_length, window=self.window)
        return inverse_transform.unsqueeze(-2)

    def forward(self, input_data):
        self.magnitude, self.phase = self.transform(input_data)
        reconstruction = self.inverse(self.magnitude, self.phase)
        return reconstruction


def test_fn() -> bool:
    """Return True if NO bug. False if bug present.

    The bug: torch.compile of STFT/iSTFT with complex ops crashes on backward
    with `InductorError: AttributeError: 'complex' object has no attribute 'get_name'`.
    """
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    backend = os.environ.get("TORCH_COMPILE_BACKEND", "inductor")
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

    torch.manual_seed(42)
    model_eager = TorchSTFT(device=device)
    model_compiled = torch.compile(TorchSTFT(device=device), backend=backend)

    x_eager = torch.randn(16000, requires_grad=True, device=device)
    x_compiled = x_eager.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)

    y_eager = model_eager(x_eager)
    y_compiled = model_compiled(x_compiled)

    y_eager.sum().backward()
    y_compiled.sum().backward()

    if not torch.allclose(y_eager, y_compiled, atol=1e-4):
        return False
    if not torch.allclose(x_eager.grad, x_compiled.grad, atol=1e-4):
        return False
    return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        ok = test_fn()
        print(f"test_fn returned: {ok}")
    except Exception:
        import traceback
        traceback.print_exc()
        os._exit(2)
    os._exit(0 if ok else 1)

issues.title: 🐛 torch.compile silently bypasses dtype mismatch checks in SFDP attention patterns
issues.author: Prorrrice
issues.body:
`torch.compile` silently bypasses dtype mismatch checks in attention computations, while eager mode correctly raises a `RuntimeError`. This allows code with `float16 @ float32` matrix multiplication to execute silently in compiled mode, potentially producing incorrect numerical results.

When performing attention computations that involve explicit dtype conversions (e.g., converting attention weights to `float16` while keeping values in `float32`), eager mode correctly detects the type mismatch and raises an error. However, `torch.compile` bypasses this safety check and executes the operation silently.

## Minimal Reproducer

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import math

torch.manual_seed(0)

class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_heads=8, head_dim=64, dropout_p=0.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.head_dim = head_dim
        self.dropout_p = dropout_p
        self.q_proj = nn.Linear(head_dim * num_heads, head_dim * num_heads)
        self.k_proj = nn.Linear(head_dim * num_heads, head_dim * num_heads)
        self.v_proj = nn.Linear(head_dim * num_heads, head_dim * num_heads)
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(head_dim * num_heads, head_dim * num_heads)

    def forward(self, x):
        batch_size, seq_len, _ = x.shape
        q = self.q_proj(x).reshape(batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.head_dim)
        k = self.k_proj(x).reshape(batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.head_dim)
        v = self.v_proj(x).reshape(batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.head_dim)
        q = q.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        k = k.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        v = v.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        
        # Compute attention scores
        div = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(q.size(-1))
        div = div.to(torch.float32)  # Convert to float32
        attn_weight = torch.softmax(div, dim=-1)
        attn_weight = torch.dropout(attn_weight, self.dropout_p, False)
        attn_weight = attn_weight.to(torch.float16)  # Convert to float16
        
        # BUG: attn_weight is float16, v is float32 - dtype mismatch!
        output = attn_weight @ v
        
        output = output.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(batch_size, seq_len, -1)
        output = self.out_proj(output)
        return output

func = Model().cuda().eval()
x = torch.randn(2, 16, 512).cuda()

with torch.no_grad():
    # Eager mode - correctly raises error
    print("Eager mode:")
    try:
        result = func(x.clone())
        print(f"  Output shape: {result.shape}")
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"  RuntimeError: {e}")
    
    # Compiled mode - silently succeeds (BUG!)
    print("\nCompiled mode:")
    func1 = torch.compile(func)
    try:
        result = func1(x.clone())
        print(f"  Output shape: {result.shape}, dtype: {result.dtype}")
        print("  WARNING: Compiled mode bypassed dtype check!")
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"  RuntimeError: {e}")
```

## Expected behavior

Both eager and compiled modes should behave consistently:
- **Option 1**: Both raise `RuntimeError: expected scalar type Half but found Float`
- **Option 2**: Both perform implicit type promotion and succeed

Currently, the inconsistency is a significant bug because users cannot rely on `torch.compile` to maintain the same safety guarantees as eager mode.

## Actual behavior

| Mode | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| Eager mode | ✅ Correctly raises `RuntimeError: expected scalar type Half but found Float` |
| Compiled mode | ❌ **Silently succeeds**, bypassing dtype safety check |

## Root Cause Analysis

The issue appears to be in the Inductor compiler's handling of dtype conversions in SFDP (Scaled Dot Product Attention) patterns. During graph optimization, the compiler may:

1. Fuse operations in a way that skips runtime dtype validation
2. Apply implicit type promotion without user awareness
3. Generate Triton kernels that accept mismatched dtypes

This is particularly dangerous because:
- Users may not notice the silent dtype mismatch
- Numerical precision issues may go undetected
- The behavior differs between eager and compiled modes

## Potential Impact

1. **Precision Loss**: float16 × float32 may produce unexpected results
2. **Silent Errors**: No warning or error in production code
3. **Debugging Difficulty**: Hard to trace numerical issues back to dtype mismatch
4. **Semantic Inconsistency**: torch.compile changes program semantics

## Error logs

**Eager mode output:**
```
RuntimeError: expected scalar type Half but found Float
```

**Compiled mode output:**
```
Output shape: torch.Size([2, 16, 512]), dtype: torch.float32
WARNING: Compiled mode bypassed dtype check!
```

## Versions

issues.title: `torch.compile` produces wrong results when `F.layer_norm` is fused with `reciprocal`/`rsqrt` epilogue
issues.author: wuyii8941
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


## Summary

When Inductor fuses `F.layer_norm` with a subsequent division-like pointwise op (`reciprocal`, `rsqrt`, `1/sqrt`), the generated kernel produces significantly wrong results. Each op alone compiles correctly; only the fused combination triggers the bug. `aot_eager` produces correct results, confirming this is an Inductor codegen issue.

## Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.randn(64, 128, device='cuda')

def fn(x):
    return torch.reciprocal(torch.abs(F.layer_norm(x, [128])) + 1e-6)

eager = fn(x)

torch._dynamo.reset()
aot = torch.compile(fn, backend='aot_eager')(x)

torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend='inductor')(x)

print(f"eager vs aot_eager: {(eager - aot).abs().max().item():.4e}")    # 0.0000e+00
print(f"eager vs inductor:  {(eager - compiled).abs().max().item():.4e}")  # ~9e-01
```

## Affected ops (epilogue after `layer_norm`)

| Epilogue op | Triggers? | Max diff |
|-------------|-----------|----------|
| `reciprocal` | Yes | ~80 (shape dependent) |
| `rsqrt` | Yes | ~877 (with cummax prefix) |
| `1/sqrt` (manual) | Yes | ~0.05 |
| `exp` | No | ~7e-6 |
| `tanh` | No | ok |

## Trigger conditions

- **Op pattern**: `F.layer_norm(x, [N])` followed by `reciprocal`, `rsqrt`, or `1/sqrt`
- **Shape dependent**: larger tensors trigger more reliably; small tensors (e.g., `(2, 256)`) may not trigger
- **dtype**: primarily float32; float16 also affected; float64 and bfloat16 appear unaffected
- **Backend**: Inductor only; `aot_eager` is correct
- **Each op alone is correct**: `layer_norm` alone is correct (diff ~7e-7), `reciprocal`/`rsqrt` alone on LN output is correct (diff = 0)
- **Manual normalization does not trigger**: `x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps)` + `rsqrt` is fine — only `F.layer_norm` triggers

## Amplified by upstream scan ops

When `cummax`/`cummin`/`cumsum` precedes the pattern, the error is amplified dramatically because the scan output distribution differs from random normal:

```python
x = torch.randn(68, 4, 14, 9, device='cuda')

def fn(x):
    t = torch.cummax(x, dim=-1)[0]         # scan op
    t = F.layer_norm(t, [9])                # layer_norm
    return torch.rsqrt(torch.abs(t) + 1e-6) # rsqrt epilogue

eager = fn(x)
torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend='inductor')(x)
print((eager - compiled).abs().max().item())  # ~877
```

## Shape sensitivity

```
# reciprocal(|LN(x)| + eps), varying shape:
(32, 64)      → diff=0.011
(64, 128)     → diff=0.82
(32, 32, 32)  → diff=81
(8, 4, 14, 9) → diff=0.077
```



### Versions


## Environment

- PyTorch: 2.13.0.dev20260601+cu126
- GPU: NVIDIA Tesla T4 (CUDA 12.6)
- OS: Linux

issues.title: `@torch.compiler.nested_compile_region` failing on a custom op with mutations
issues.author: IlyasMoutawwakil
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

custom op with mutations fail compilation under @torch.compiler.nested_compile_region
```
    Found a custom (non-ATen) operator whose output has alias annotations:
    repro::add_into(Tensor(a0!) d, Tensor x) -> ().
    We only support functionalizing operators whose outputs do not have alias
    annotations.
```
```python

import torch


@torch.library.custom_op("repro::add_into", mutates_args=("d",))
def add_into(d: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    """Compile-aware in-place add: ``d.add_(x)``."""
    d.add_(x)


@add_into.register_fake
def _add_into_fake(d, x):  # noqa: ARG001
    return None


# --- Scenario A: same op, called at top level (no nested_compile_region) ----


def top_level(d: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    torch.ops.repro.add_into(d, x)
    return d + 1.0


# --- Scenario B: same op, called from inside nested_compile_region ----------


@torch.compiler.nested_compile_region
def nested_inner(d: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    torch.ops.repro.add_into(d, x)
    return d + 1.0


def with_nested(d: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return nested_inner(d, x)


def main() -> int:
    d = torch.zeros(4, device="cpu")
    x = torch.ones(4, device="cpu")

    # Sanity: eager.
    print("eager top_level   :", top_level(d.clone(), x))
    print("eager with_nested :", with_nested(d.clone(), x))

    failures = 0

    # Scenario A: top-level torch.compile — expected to PASS.
    print()
    print("--- Scenario A: torch.compile(top_level)  [no nested_compile_region] ---")
    compiled_a = torch.compile(top_level, fullgraph=True)
    try:
        out = compiled_a(d.clone(), x)
        print(f"PASS — compiled top-level: {out}")
    except Exception as e:
        failures += 1
        print(f"UNEXPECTED FAIL ({type(e).__name__}): {e}")

    # Scenario B: nested_compile_region inside torch.compile — expected to FAIL on torch 2.12.
    print()
    print("--- Scenario B: torch.compile(with_nested)  [calls nested_compile_region] ---")
    compiled_b = torch.compile(with_nested, fullgraph=True)
    try:
        out = compiled_b(d.clone(), x)
        print(f"PASS — compiled with nested: {out}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"FAIL ({type(e).__name__}): {e}")
        failures += 1

    print()
    if failures == 1:
        print(
            "Summary: top-level works, nested_compile_region path fails — bug confirmed."
        )
        return 0
    print(f"Summary: unexpected outcome (failures={failures}).")
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
```

The '(a)' is the alias annotation). The alias annotation specifies that the output Tensor shares storage with an input that has the same annotation. comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
**Claude finished @jansel's task in 9m 13s** —— [View job](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/27231514897)

---
### Where this was fixed

@jansel I traced the fix in the code on `main`. Short version: the bug was fixed by **adding `auto_functionalize` support to `invoke_subgraph` (and HOPs generally)**, so a subgraph that mutates its inputs is now routed through `do_auto_functionalize_v2` instead of being passed verbatim to functionalization (which is what produced the `output has alias annotations` error).

#### Root cause
On torch 2.12, `invoke_subgraph`'s functionalization key assumed the subgraph was already functional — *"There is an assumption that subgraph does not mutate inputs and there is no aliasing. It's Dynamo's responsibility to prevent formation of invoke_subgraph ops if input aliasing/mutation is detected."* When a custom op with `mutates_args` lived inside the region, that assumption broke and the mutating op was handed straight to the functionalize pass, which rejects custom ops whose schema carries a write/alias annotation (`Tensor(a0!)`).

#### The fix (on `main`)
`torch/_higher_order_ops/invoke_subgraph.py:1020-1099` — the `py_functionalize_impl` now builds a `HopInstance`, and if `can_auto_functionalize(hop_instance)` is true it returns `do_auto_functionalize_v2(...)`:

```python
if can_auto_functionalize(hop_instance):
    # NOTE: [auto_functionalize x invoke_subgraph caching]
    # We call auto_functionalized_v2 to support input mutation of invoke_subgraph.
    # See NOTE [Support input mutation of hops] for the overall design.
    ...
    return do_auto_functionalize_v2(
        ctx.mode, hop_instance,
        (subgraph, "auto_functionalized_" + identifier, *operands), {},
    )
```

The overall design is documented in **`NOTE [Support input mutation of hops]`** at `torch/_higher_order_ops/base_hop.py:133-150`: functionalize the subgraph, inline a `copy_` epilogue, route the HOP through `auto_functionalized_v2`, and let inductor decompose it — the same machinery custom ops already use for input mutation. The matching `can_auto_functionalize(HopInstance)` branch is at `torch/_higher_order_ops/auto_functionalize.py:426-445`.

Regression tests covering exactly your scenario now live in `test/higher_order_ops/test_invoke_subgraph.py`: `test_input_mutation`, `test_input_mutation_mutiple_times`, `test_input_mutation_mutiple_times_fake_tensor_cache_hit`, `test_input_mutation_inference_mode` (lines ~1357-1455).

#### Pinning the exact PR/commit
I couldn't pull the exact PR number from here — this CI checkout is a shallow clone (depth 1), and `gh`/`curl`/`WebFetch`/`git fetch` are all blocked by an ungranted permission prompt in this environment, so I can't query GitHub history. To find it locally, blame the auto_functionalize hook:

```bash
git log --oneline -L /can_auto_functionalize/,+15:torch/_higher_order_ops/invoke_subgraph.py
git log -S "auto_functionalized x invoke_subgraph caching" -- torch/_higher_order_ops/invoke_subgraph.py
git log -S "Support input mutation of hops" -- torch/_higher_order_ops/base_hop.py
git log --oneline -- test/higher_order_ops/test_invoke_subgraph.py | head   # find when test_input_mutation landed
```

(@ydwu4 authored the "input mutation of hops" / auto_functionalize-for-HOPs work and would know the exact PR.)

#### Workaround for torch 2.11 / 2.12 (no nightly)
The `auto_functionalize` machinery wasn't wired into `invoke_subgraph` on 2.12, so you can't get the region to functionalize the mutation itself. Options:

1. **Use `auto_functionalized` semantics at the op boundary.** Custom-op input mutation *does* work at the top level on 2.12 (your Scenario A passes) because top-level functionalization handles `mutates_args` via `auto_functionalized`. The region is the only thing missing that path — so keep the mutating op *outside* `nested_compile_region` and only put pure computation inside it.
2. **Make the region functional.** Return the new tensor from the region instead of mutating in place, and do the in-place write outside:
   ```python
   @nested_compile_region
   def nested_inner(d, x):
       return d + x + 1.0   # no mutation inside the region
   ```
3. If you must mutate inside, drop `nested_compile_region` for that callsite on 2.12 — top-level `torch.compile` handles the mutating custom op correctly.

issues.title: Inefficient triton kernels generated by inductor
issues.author: shunting314
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I gathered all the 10K triton kernels generated by inductor using stack of PR ( https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/120048 ). After deduping same kernels used by different fx.Graph, we get about 2K unique kernels: https://gist.github.com/shunting314/161aa8031c8cca6744a56999d74c2b47 

Note that, the data is augmented with ncu output. For each row, we have columns like ncu_duration_us, ncu_mem_bw_gbps for latency captured by ncu and memory bandwidth usage of the kernel captured by ncu.

We can do various analysis from the metadata file, but one thing that may be helpful is to run a query like
```
select count(*) from kernels where cast(ncu_duration_us as decimal) > 100 and cast(ncu_mem_bw_gbps as decimal) < 500 and cast(num_atomic_add as decimal) = 0;
```

This gives us super inefficient kernels (since membw < 500GBPS) that still run long enough time (>100us). We skip kernels using atomic_add since the benchmarking result for those kernel are bad because of contention in atomic_add.

For the kernels gathered for huggingface, there are only 14 such inefficient kernels: https://gist.github.com/shunting314/45b43cb6c03e93cd7865185a5b1d818a . 

I picked the 4th kernel: 

https://gist.github.com/shunting314/2a0bb5b1668f79caeb5b7d3df2ce5561

```
@triton.jit

comments.body:
Chatted with Hongtao and also dig more on `tl.rand` inefficiency. In triton tl.rand is implemented via philox: we generate 4 random number (more specifically 4 blocks of random numbers) each time but drop 3 ..

Another variant called tl.rand4x will return all 4 random numbers generated. I tried to manually change the triton kernel to leverage tl.rand4x:

```
@triton.jit
def new_triton_poi_fused_native_dropout_16(in_ptr0, out_ptr1, load_seed_offset, xnumel, XBLOCK : tl.constexpr):                                                           
    xnumel = 25214976
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    span: tl.constexpr = XBLOCK // 4
    tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + load_seed_offset)

    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, span)[:]
    x0 = xindex
    tmp1 = x0
    tmp20, tmp21, tmp22, tmp23 = tl.rand4x(tmp0, (tmp1).to(tl.uint32))
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    tmp2 = tmp20
    tmp3 = tmp2.to(tl.float32)
    tmp4 = 0.1
    tmp5 = tmp3 > tmp4
    tl.store(out_ptr1 + (x0), tmp5, None)

    xindex = xindex + span
    x0 = xindex
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    tmp2 = tmp21
    tmp3 = tmp2.to(tl.float32)
    tmp4 = 0.1
    tmp5 = tmp3 > tmp4
    tl.store(out_ptr1 + (x0), tmp5, None)

    xindex = xindex + span
    x0 = xindex
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    tmp2 = tmp22
    tmp3 = tmp2.to(tl.float32)
    tmp4 = 0.1
    tmp5 = tmp3 > tmp4
    tl.store(out_ptr1 + (x0), tmp5, None)

    xindex = xindex + span
    x0 = xindex
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    tmp2 = tmp23
    tmp3 = tmp2.to(tl.float32)
    tmp4 = 0.1
    tmp5 = tmp3 > tmp4
    tl.store(out_ptr1 + (x0), tmp5, None)
```
This basically duplicate the code 4 times but each time handles 1/4 elements. The benefits is we do philox computation 1/4 times.

This change improve the perf of the kernel from 136us to 56 us (2.43x improvement). But I think instead of doing the above in inductor, maybe it's better to let triton handle it so inductor does not need to do this kind of codegen. cc @htyu
